cues.text: A Slip on a Flooded Plank
On Holy Thursday, March 25, 1255, a priest of Regensburg (then known as Ratisbon) carried the Blessed Sacrament to a dying parishioner.
He came upon a stream swollen by an unexpected storm; crossing its narrow plank bridge, he slipped and dropped the ciborium, spilling the consecrated Hosts onto the bank.

The parishioners, hearing of the accident, resolved that same day to build a chapel on the site as an act of reparation for the loss; the small chapel of St. Savior was consecrated within months, on September 8, 1255.

Within that same chapel, tradition holds, a priest celebrating Mass found himself assailed by private doubts about the Real Presence at the very moment of the elevation, and hesitated over the chalice rather than lift it as the rite required.
At that moment, the account relates, the wooden figure of Christ on the altar crucifix stirred: one arm detached from the cross and reached forward.
It gently drew the chalice from the doubting priest's hands, holding the Eucharist aloft for the whole congregation to see.
Before the chalice was returned to him, the priest, in tears, begged forgiveness.
The crucifix tradition credits with this sign remains preserved in Regensburg today, drawing pilgrims who come to venerate a wooden figure.
It is said to have steadied, twice over, the wavering hands of a servant of the altar—first a priest who merely stumbled on a flooded plank, and then one who doubted outright.
Both met, in the account handed down, not with rebuke but with a sign gentle enough to restore rather than shame.
